Leveraging high-memory nodes and a mature GPU software ecosystem on Kestrel with the scale afforded by Perlmutter, researchers ran high- fidelity simulations of structures ranging between a few and 150 atoms (molecular systems and nanostructured materials) and explored methods that offer exceptional accuracy while scaling to larger, more realistic material systems run on Frontier. Researchers’ Science25 publication on molybdenum oxide dichloride revealed new insights into its surface behavior and potential for energy applications, showcasing how bridging NLR’s HPC resources with DOE leadership-class computing is accelerating scientific discovery and technological innovation. Their adoption in mission-critical applications requires knowing how much to trust their predictions. To address this, NLR researchers developed methods to estimate and propagate uncertainty arising both from noisy data (aleatoric uncertainty) and from data gaps in training datasets (epistemic uncertainty). Initiated through DOE’s Computational Science Graduate Fellowship and later funded by DOE’s ASCR program, this work resulted in a general framework for propagation of uncertainty through expensive forward models. Researchers used Bayesian neural networks to test uncertainty estimation approaches on reactive flow problems, including unsteady flame flashback.
